Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A shaggy highland cow standing in tall golden-green grass at sunset, with violet hills, a sliver of loch and a gold and blue sky behind

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

22 stepsCanvas: 12 x 16 inFocal point: The cow's face: the pink nose under the long gold-lit fringe, framed by the two curved horns Light: A low sun behind the cow and to the right, near the horizon: the sky glows gold low on the right, and the light catches the top of the cow's fringe and the right-hand edge of its coat as a bright gold rimHow this lesson was made

Before you start

You're about to paint a shaggy highland cow standing in tall golden grass at sunset, with violet hills and a glint of loch behind. What makes it sing is the cow's face: the pink nose peeking out of a long, glowing fringe, framed by two curved horns.

The light

The low sun sits behind the cow, near the horizon. It turns the sky gold where it sets, catches the edges of things, and wraps a bright gold rim round the cow's fringe and coat while its face and body stay in warm shadow.

What this painting teaches

  • Dry brush (steps 2, 3, 5, 22). A nearly dry brush skimmed lightly so the paint breaks up on the canvas. It makes the cloud streaks, the shadowed hollows of the hills and the last glowing rim on the cow. Wipe the brush well: too much paint and it goes on solid.
  • Thick to thin (steps 13, 14). Press the full width of the angle brush, then lift onto its edge as you pull, so each mark tapers to a point. Every hanging lock of the cow's coat is one of these. Lift at the end, or the locks look blunt and stuck on.
  • Flicking (steps 19, 20, 21). A quick upward stroke with the fan brush that lifts off as it goes, so each blade thins at its tip. It builds the tall grass in passes, darkest first. Keep the load light, or the blades turn into flat blobs.

The way there

We start at the back: the sunset sky in one wet blend, then its clouds. The far hills and the loch go on next, then the green hillside, its bushes and the meadow, so the whole background is done fast. The first layers stop short where the next one covers them, so bare canvas showing early on is expected. Most of the time goes on the cow: a flat shape, shading, then two passes of hanging locks before the horns and the face. The tall grass is flicked over the cow's legs after, so it stands in the field. The brightest gold goes on last, when everything it covers is dry.

This lesson skips about a whole canvas of painting that later layers would cover.

Placing shapes with a transfer outline optional

Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The sky 3 steps

The farthest thing first: a smooth sunset sky with soft cloud streaks across it.

Where: Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is about 5 in from the top edge.

STEP 1 OF 22 · The sky, 1 of 3

Blend the sunset sky

  • Start: Start along the top edge of the canvas with Sky blue, stroking side to side from the left edge to the right edge.
  • Strokes: Work down in level strokes. Without rinsing, work in Pale gold next as you go down, then Golden yellow, and stroke back up over each join while wet.
  • Where the paint sits: The blue stays at the top and the Golden yellow sits lowest, running lower on the right side of the sky, where the sun is. A hard line means: add the lighter color and blend again.
  • Leave: The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 4.
  • Stop when: A smooth blue-to-gold sky. Its lower edge is loose and uneven, not ruled: about 3 3/4 in from the top edge for most of its width, about 6 in from the top edge at the right edge.

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
Basics: Colors dry darker

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. Creamy paint. An even coat.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 22 · The sky, 2 of 3

Dry-brush the orange cloud streaks

  • First: Let the sky dry completely first.
  • Start: Start about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, skimming a long, flat-bottomed streak of Peach orange across the sky.
  • As in step 1: The Golden yellow from the sky comes back, but now dry-brushed in broken streaks instead of blended smooth.
  • Strokes: Wipe the brush nearly dry and skim sideways with light pressure, so each streak breaks up on the canvas. Lay Golden yellow streaks in among them.
  • Where the paint sits: The streaks stack in loose rows down the sky, more on the right side of the sky, where the sun is low. A few short ones reach the sky's lower edge.
  • Leave: Let the sky show between the streaks and through their broken edges. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 4.
  • Stop when: Soft orange and gold streaks lie across the sky. If one goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

Stroke: Dry brush how to do it, not checked yet

Dry brush

Not checked yet

With. flat; old stiff flat (catches the canvas weave best)

Load. Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.

Motion. Light pressure, skimming the surface.

What it leaves. Feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.

Then. Build up in several light passes.

Good for. cloud highlights, grass, wood and fences, highlights on round things

Skim, with almost no paint

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.

Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 22 · The sky, 3 of 3

Light the tops of the clouds

  • First: Let the cloud streaks dry first.
  • Start: Start near the top edge on the left side of the sky, skimming Pale gold along the upper edge of the highest streak.
  • As in step 2: The same dry brush as the streaks, but with even less paint, and only where the sun catches their edges.
  • Strokes: Use a dry brush with almost no paint and skim sideways along the top of each streak in one light pass.
  • Where the paint sits: Touch only upper edges, where the low sun catches the clouds: a thin line on the highest streaks, and a longer, softer one low in the sky, its top about 3 1/2 in from the top edge.
  • Leave: Leave the orange showing in each streak, and most streaks untouched. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 4.
  • Stop when: A few streaks have a faint pale glow along their tops. If it reads as new white clouds, you pressed too hard.

The far hills and the loch 3 steps

Distance: pale and darker violet hills, shaded so they roll back, with a sliver of water at their foot.

Where: Inside the outlined area, all the way across. Its top is about 2 in from the top edge and its bottom is about 5 in from the top edge.

STEP 4 OF 22 · The far hills and the loch, 1 of 3

Lay in the far violet hills

  • First: Let the sky dry first.
  • Start: Start with the Hazy lavender range, its rolling tops about 2 1/4 in from the top edge, along the bottom of the sky.
  • Strokes: Bend each stroke down along the curve of each bump. Then lay the Hill violet range in front, its tops a little lower, overlapping the lavender.
  • Where the paint sits: The lavender shows only as the back row of soft tops; Hill violet covers the rest, since nearer land reads darker. Keep both flat.
  • Leave: Small gaps of sky left in the violet are fine; step 5 fills them. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 7.
  • Stop when: Two flat violet ranges. The lower edge is loose and uneven: about 5 1/4 in from the top edge for most of its width, about 6 in from the top edge at the right edge.

Curved strokes

Not checked yet

Motion. Bend every stroke with the shape: from the top of each bump down along its curve, and around a round shape.

What it leaves. Marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.

Then. Use the darker mix along the shadow side and the lighter one along the lit side, both following the curve.

Good for. hills, pumpkin ribs, a balloon

STEP 5 OF 22 · The far hills and the loch, 2 of 3

Shade the far hills' slopes

  • First: Let the violet hills dry first.
  • Start: Start in the middle of the nearer range, about 3 1/4 in from the top edge, dry-brushing Deep violet just under its rolling tops.
  • As in step 2: The same dry brush you used on the clouds, now with the bigger brush, building dark hollows on the hills instead of streaks.
  • Strokes: Skim the nearly dry brush lightly along each slope in a few short passes, building the dark in light layers.
  • Where the paint sits: The dark sits in hollows just under the nearer ridges, most of it on the right side of the far violet hills, with two small patches at the left edge.
  • Leave: Leave the pale back range and the ridge tops showing. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 7.
  • Stop when: The nearer range has dark hollows, so it reads as hills one behind another, and the gaps from step 4 are filled.

STEP 6 OF 22 · The far hills and the loch, 3 of 3

Lay in the sliver of loch

  • First: Let the hills dry first.
  • Start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, at the foot of the far violet hills, with a thin band of Pale gold.
  • As in step 1: You blended this Pale gold into the sky. Here it becomes the water, so the loch mirrors the sunset.
  • Strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long, flat strokes in from the right edge, tapering the band to a point about 9 3/4 in from the left edge.
  • Where the paint sits: Lay a thin line of Hill violet along the top edge of the gold for the far shore. The rest stays bright gold: still water catching the sunset.
  • Leave: Leave the violet hills showing around the loch. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 7.
  • Stop when: A bright sliver of loch about 2 1/4 in wide, with a violet shore along its top.

The hillside and the meadow 4 steps

The ground the cow will stand on: a green hillside dotted with bushes and a glowing meadow base.

Where: Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 3 in from the top edge.

STEP 7 OF 22 · The hillside and the meadow, 1 of 4

Lay in the green hillside

  • First: Let the hills and the loch dry first.
  • Start: Start at the left edge just below the far violet hills, and run the hillside's curving ridge down toward the loch at the right edge.
  • As in step 6: The same long, level strokes as the loch, now with the big brush across the whole hillside.
  • Strokes: Pull long, level strokes left and right with Olive green, working down band by band to the bottom edge.
  • Where the paint sits: Work Gold-green into the upper slopes and in soft bands across the hillside, where the low sun lies. Keep more Olive green lower down, with a few darker patches.
  • Leave: Leave the far hills and the loch showing. The hillside's top covers the hills' loose lower edge.
  • Stop when: No white canvas shows. The hillside is olive with gold-green bands, its curving top about 3 1/4 in from the top edge at its highest.

STEP 8 OF 22 · The hillside and the meadow, 2 of 4

Dab the dark bushes on the hillside

  • First: Let the hillside dry first, or the dabs turn to mud.
  • Start: Start along the ridge at the left edge, tapping Dark green just under the ridge line, and work along it toward the right edge.
  • Strokes: Tap with the tip of the stiff brush, no water on it. Build each bush as a clump of taps, in rows that slope with the hillside.
  • Where the paint sits: Most bushes sit in rows on the upper hillside, the first row about 3 1/4 in from the top edge, smaller toward the back. A few bigger patches go near the bottom edge.
  • Leave: Leave plenty of the olive and gold hillside showing between the rows and the bushes.
  • Stop when: Dark scrubby patches dot the hillside in rows. Blobs mean the brush is too wet: wipe it on a paper towel.

STEP 13 OF 22 · The shaggy coat, 1 of 2

Pull the copper locks

  • First: Let the shading dry first.
  • Start: Start at the crown of the head, pressing the brush flat and pulling the fringe locks down over the face.
  • Strokes: Press the full width, then lift onto the edge as you pull down, so each lock tapers to a point. Work down the body in overlapping rows.
  • Where the paint sits: Cover the fringe, the top of the head and the whole body with Light copper locks. On the body they hang down and curve with its roundness.
  • Leave: Leave thin gaps of the dark shading from step 12 between locks so they read as hair. Leave the lighter patch on the face and chest alone.
  • Stop when: The cow is covered in long copper locks with dark between them. Blunt ends mean you didn't lift.

Line in the eye, nostrils and mouth

Liner work

With. liner; small round (the tip)

Load. Thin paint. Swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Add water if the line skips. Reload often.

Then. Reload often.

The low sun's brightest touches, put on last over dry paint.

Where: Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 2 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 11 in wide and 9 in tall.

STEP 22 OF 22 · The last lights, 1 of 1

Dry-brush the brightest sunlit edges

  • First: Let everything dry completely first.
  • Start: Start along the top of the fringe between the horns, dry-brushing short Pale gold strokes that run off the edge of the hair.
  • As in step 3: You skimmed this Pale gold onto the clouds' sunlit edges. Now it goes on the edges the sun hits, with the smallest flat.
  • Strokes: Wipe the brush nearly dry and skim short strokes outward across the edge, so the light looks fuzzy, not drawn.
  • Where the paint sits: Light the rim along the head and back, down the lit side of the chest, and a thin line on top of each horn. Skim a glow across the back of the meadow and tip a few seed heads.
  • Leave: Leave the shaded side of the cow, its face and most of the grass untouched.
  • Stop when: A gold rim glows along the cow's top and lit side, the horns catch a line of light, and the back of the meadow shines.
Paints for this step1 paint
  • Pale gold (Golden yellow plus white) from step 1, mix more if it has dried6 parts white, 2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part ultramarine, a touch of yellow

Brushes

1/4 inch flat

Stroke: Dry brush, as in step 2.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A highland cow standing in tall grass at sunset, far hills and a sliver of loch behind

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: Nothing in the image is outside the scene.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 12 x 16 in, portrait

Done: crop

Left out: about a ninth of the photo, thin strips at the top of the sky and the bottom of the grass

Why: The default size closest to the photo's shape; the whole cow with both horn tips and some sky stay.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: no (only small rocks on the left hillside). Textures of hundreds of items: yes, the tall grass blades and seed stalks across the bottom third and the hair strands of the coat; busy measured 13.1% fine texture, mostly in the bottom grass and the fringe. Detail inside big shapes: yes, the coat's strands and the wispy clouds. More parts than 8: no, about 7.

Changed: Grass across the bottom third as loose upward flicks in three greens with golden tips and a few broad seed-head dabs, no thin stalks; stalks crossing the legs and chest dropped; the coat as big wavy locks in dark rust, mid ginger and a golden rim; the fringe as three or four locks; the horns as two smooth cream curves; the hillside rocks dropped; the far hills as three soft bands; the clouds as two or three soft streaks.

Why: Every step is erased back from the finish, so each blade and strand would have to be painted. Fine texture fell from 13.1% to 1.1%; nothing on the list survived; the cow, horns, hills, loch and sunset light are all there. No redo.

Fine texture measured: the photo 13.1%, the beginner version 1.1%, the finish 0.2% of the canvas

One big shaggy cow standing in tall grass at sunset, lit from behind and to the right, with a glowing sky, soft violet hills and a green hillside behind. What matters is the cow's mass and its glowing rim; what's hard is the coat, which has to read as hanging locks a beginner can pull, not strands. The lesson should get the background on fast and spend its time on the cow.

Subject: A shaggy highland cow standing in tall golden-green grass at sunset, with violet hills, a sliver of loch and a gold and blue sky behind
Focal point: The cow's face: the pink nose under the long gold-lit fringe, framed by the two curved horns
Light: A low sun behind the cow and to the right, near the horizon: the sky glows gold low on the right, and the light catches the top of the cow's fringe and the right-hand edge of its coat as a bright gold rim

What it saw, back to front

  1. The sunset sky
  2. The loch
  3. The green hillside
  4. The tall-grass meadow
  5. The highland cow
  6. The horns
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

A sunset sky, far hills and a grassy field behind one big cow paint naturally back to front on white canvas, and every texture here (cloud streaks, dabbed bushes, hanging locks, flicked grass) is one repeated mark.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner.yaml)

It has no version 2 keys, so the pipeline can't plan with it.

How the paint recipes were worked out17 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order22 steps

Back to front: the sky and its clouds, the far hills and the loch, the hillside and the meadow base, then the cow (shape, shading, two passes of locks), its horns and face, the tall grass flicked over its legs, and the brightest lights last. With pipeline v4's rule the sky, clouds and far hills stop at loose lines where later layers will cover them, so the bare canvas below waits for the far hills (step 4) and the hillside (step 7).

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky

    The farthest thing first, blended wet in one go; it stops at a loose line about 3 3/4 in down because the hills and hillside cover the rest.

  2. 2. Dry-brush the orange cloud streaks

    The cloud streaks go on the dry sky, before anything in front of them.

  3. 3. Light the tops of the clouds

    The sunlit tops come after the streaks they sit on.

  4. 4. Lay in the far violet hills

    The farthest land next, flat, stopping where the hillside will cover it.

  5. 5. Shade the far hills' slopes

    Shadows in the hills after their flat colors are dry.

  6. 6. Lay in the sliver of loch

    The water at the foot of the far hills, before the hillside in front of it.

  7. 7. Lay in the green hillside

    The ground runs to the bottom edge so the meadow and the cow are painted over it.

  8. 8. Dab the dark bushes on the hillside

    Texture on the hillside after its base: the dark taps first.

  9. 9. Dab the sunlit tops of the bushes

    The lit taps on top of the dark, covering less.

  10. 10. Blend the meadow base

    The base under the tall grass before the cow, so the cow stands in it.

  11. 11. Block in the cow from pieces

    The subject's flat shape over the finished background.

  12. 12. Shade the cow's coat

    The cow's darker side before its coat texture.

  13. 13. Pull the copper locks

    The coat's first pass of locks, following the body.

  14. 14. Pull the golden locks

    Fewer, lighter locks over the first pass.

  15. 15. Build the horns from curved pieces

    The horns after the coat, so the fringe can overlap their bases.

  16. 16. Shade the horn bases

    Shading inside the horns once they're dry.

  17. 17. Paint the pink nose

    The face's one light shape before its dark details.

  18. 18. Line in the eye, nostrils and mouth

    The darkest small marks last on the face.

  19. 19. Flick the dark grass

    Grass in front of the cow goes on after it, dark first.

  20. 20. Flick the olive grass

    A lighter pass of the same flicks.

  21. 21. Flick the golden seed heads

    The seed heads on top of the grass.

  22. 22. Dry-brush the brightest sunlit edges

    The brightest rim lights last, when everything under them is dry.

Filters it tried5 free looks
Where Claude drew diagrams2 steps, free

Read each step as a first-time painter with only its picture and words. Two steps make a shape appear whole (the cow, the horns) and get a diagram; the rest are fills, repeated marks, or small shapes the words place. The words matched the pictures, including the stopped sky and hills and the bare canvas below them, so no line was changed.

  • Step 11: Block in the cow from pieces beginner check

    Noticed: An animal appears whole in one step; the outline (body, head, shoulder, rump, legs) is hard to start from the picture alone.

    Pieces: The body as one big oval first, then the head as a rounded piece at the top right, then ( ) pieces for the shoulder and rump and two short legs, as the words say.

  • Step 15: Build the horns from curved pieces beginner check

    Noticed: Two narrow curved shapes whose start and bend aren't obvious from the picture.

    Pieces: A wide base piece at each side of the head, then thinner pieces curving up to a point: the left one taller, the right one curling out and up.

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A blended fill; the words give where it stops.
  • Step 2: Streaks made by repeating one dry-brush mark.
  • Step 3: Dry-brush on the top edges of streaks already there.
  • Step 4: Flat bands; the words give the ridge height and where they stop.
  • Step 5: Soft dry-brush in hollows already painted.
  • Step 6: One thin strip the words place.
  • Step 7: Long level bands, one repeated stroke.
  • Step 8: Repeated taps in rows.
  • Step 9: The same taps, lighter, on top.
  • Step 10: A blended fill.
  • Step 12: Curved strokes on the shape already there.
  • Step 13: One repeated thick-to-thin mark following the body.
  • Step 14: The same mark, fewer and lighter.
  • Step 16: Shading inside the horns already there.
  • Step 17: One small rounded shape the words size and place.
  • Step 18: Dots and short lines on the nose and fringe.
  • Step 19: Repeated flicks.
  • Step 20: Repeated flicks.
  • Step 21: Repeated short flicks.
  • Step 22: A few dry-brush touches.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Helpers, and what each was given. Plan writer (Opus): v3/plan-brief.md, the lesson folder, 00_beginner.png and the technique file; it wrote plan.json and fixed plan-check's three missing unit names itself. Chain checker (Opus): v3/chain-check.md and chain/looks; it marked nothing. Lesson writer (Opus): words/lesson (brief.md, then feedback.md once, then arc-brief.md). Steps 0, 1 and 8 were done in the session that started the run.
  • Pipeline v4 (--stops): on this chain the image model painted sky, not far hills, behind the hillside, so under the rule as first adopted (line-1-next) only the far hills stopped (0.017 of a canvas). The owner widened the rule during the run (docs/decisions.md, 2026-11-21; PR #306): now the sky and clouds stop too, at about 3 3/4 in, and the lesson skips about 1 canvas.
  • Step 4: holes in the far hills' render show bare white canvas low in the hills (and a few cloud bits higher up) until step 5 shades them. The rule makes the lower ones white where they were sky before; filed in review.json.
  • Paints 'Pale gold' and 'Light copper' were fitted far from their names (build-steps' notes); left, since renaming renders part of the chain again.

Known problems

Where the pictures aren't quite right. Paint it the way the step says and use the picture as a guide.

  • Step 1, Blend the sunset sky: The paint called Pale gold was measured from the pictures as a grayish beige (#c2b1a5), not the pale warm gold its name says, so its swatch may look duller than the name.
  • Step 4, Lay in the far violet hills: Small holes in the violet show bare white canvas low in the hills and a few orange bits of cloud higher up, where the image model didn't repaint; step 5's shading covers them.
  • Step 13, Pull the copper locks: The paint called Light copper was measured from the pictures as a deep rust (#9e4d22), darker than its name says.
